2.1 For real $f$, [F3] identifies the scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ with $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)$. The Hilbert space $H_\mu$ is separable by [F13], so the hypothesis of the Segal-domain result [F4] holds. 4.1 Fix a unit spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ and, for $\varepsilon>0$, define $u_\varepsilon(\mathbf x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\rho_3((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\varepsilon)z$. For every spatial Schwartz test, change of variables and [F10] show that its pairing with $u_\varepsilon$ tends to the test's value at $\mathbf x_0$ times $z$, while $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2=\varepsilon^{-3/2}\|\rho_3\|_2\to\infty$. By [F16], choose countable dense sets in the two Dirac energy ranges. Conjugating the negative-range dense set preserves density, and the Cartesian product of the two dense sets is countable and dense in the Hilbert direct sum. Therefore the one-particle space for the CAR Fock representation is separable and [F17] applies. For $A_\varepsilon=\Psi_t(u_\varepsilon)$, [F8] gives $A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2I$. By [F17], the creation and annihilation terms are bounded, hence so is their sum. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] gives $\sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle A_\varepsilon x,y\rangle|\le\|A_\varepsilon\|$, while choosing $y=A_\varepsilon x/\|A_\varepsilon x\|$ for each unit $x$ with $A_\varepsilon x\ne0$ gives equality after taking the supremum over $x$. The adjoint identity swaps $x$ and $y$, so the same two-vector supremum equals $\|A_\varepsilon^\dagger\|$. For bounded operators $X,Y$, each unit $\xi$ satisfies $\|XY\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|\,\|Y\|$ and $\|(X+Y)\xi\|\le\|X\xi\|+\|Y\xi\|\le\|X\|+\|Y\|$; taking suprema gives product submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality. Applying these inequalities to the CAR identity yields $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\|A_\varepsilon A_\varepsilon^\dagger+A_\varepsilon^\dagger A_\varepsilon\|\le2\|A_\varepsilon\|^2$. Thus $\|A_\varepsilon\|\ge\|u_\varepsilon\|_2/\sqrt2\to\infty$, excluding a bounded equal-time point-field norm limit. [F8, F10, F12, F16, F17, F18, step 2.3, given, algebra] ∎

2.1 To apply [F2] with one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$, first verify its separability hypothesis. Let $D$ be the countable dense subset of real $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ supplied by [F4]. Its sixfold product is countable by [F5]; identifying each tuple with a three-component complex function whose real and imaginary components lie in $D$ gives a dense subset of $\mathcal H$. Density follows by approximating the six real $L^2$ components, since the squared complex-vector norm is the sum of their squared norms. Hence $\mathcal H$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6]. The image of this countable set under the bounded projection $M_{P_T}$ is countable and dense in $\mathcal H_T$: for $u\in\mathcal H_T$, $M_{P_T}u=u$, so projected approximants to $u$ converge to $u$. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6], and [F2] applies. By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given]

Here the formula is for $\mathbf k\ne0$; values at $\mathbf k=0$ are irrelevant to the integrals. The symbols $a_i(\mathbf k)$ and $a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)$ are distributional notation for the Fock maps: for Schwartz vectors $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ set $a(u):=a(P_Tu)$ and $a^\dagger(v):=a^\dagger(P_Tv)$. Then [F2] gives $[a(u),a^\dagger(v)]=\int\overline{u_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)v_j(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k\,I$, equivalently the kernel notation $[a_i(\mathbf k),a_j^\dagger(\mathbf q)]=P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\delta^3(\mathbf k-\mathbf q)I$. The mode integrals are understood after test smearing; near $\mathbf k=0$ their squared one-particle weights behave respectively as $1/\omega$ and $\omega$, both locally integrable against $d^3\mathbf k$, and at infinity the Fourier transforms of the spatial tests decrease rapidly. 1.1 Put $K=e^\perp$ and $G=\mathcal F_s(K)$ for a unit vector $e$. Since $H$ is separable, its continuous orthogonal projection $v\mapsto v-\langle e,v\rangle_2e$ sends a countable dense subset of $H$ to a countable dense subset of $K$. Finite elementary tensors from that subset have dense span in each tensor power by [F8]; applying the bounded symmetrizer gives a countable dense subset of each $K_s^{(m)}$. Rational complex finite sums over the countably many sectors give a countable dense subset of $G$ consisting of finite-particle vectors. Gram–Schmidt, omitting zero residuals, therefore gives a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)_{j\in J}$ of $G$ whose vectors are all finite-particle. [A1, F2, F8, construct]

1.2 Map the one-mode basis $|n\rangle=e^{\otimes n}$ to $g_n$. The map $V:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb Ce)\to L^2_2(\mathbb R)$ is a linear unitary: the two displayed families are complete orthonormal families, and both pairings are second-variable-linear. Here $L^2_2$ has pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$; the core and self-adjointness of $Qf=xf$ transfer from [F4] by complex conjugation. The recurrence [F3] shows that $V\,2^{-1/2}(a^\dagger(e)+a(e))V^{-1}$ equals $Q$ on the finite Hermite span. Together with $J$ [F2], the full field for $h=re$ acts in $L^2_2(\mathbb R)\widehat\otimes G$ as multiplication by $rx$ on the dense span of $g_n\otimes u_j$. [F2, F3, F4, F8, construct]

1.3 Under the product-basis unitary of [F8], identify $L^2_2(\mathbb R)\widehat\otimes G$ with $\ell^2(J;L^2_2(\mathbb R))$. Define $M_r(f_j)=(rx f_j)$ on $D(M_r)=\{(f_j):\sum_j\int r^2x^2|f_j(x)|^2dx<\infty\}$. Its domain is dense because finite coordinates supported in $[-m,m]$ are dense. It is symmetric since $rx$ is real. If $g\in D(M_r^*)$ and $k=M_r^*g$, test the adjoint identity in coordinate $j$ against $f_j=(rxg_j-k_j)\mathbf1_{[-m,m]}$ and set all other coordinates to zero. This vector lies in $D(M_r)$ because $rx$ is bounded on $[-m,m]$; the identity then gives $0=\int_{-m}^m|rxg_j-k_j|^2dx$. Letting $m\to\infty$ yields $rxg_j=k_j$ almost everywhere for each $j$, so $\sum_j\int r^2x^2|g_j|^2=\sum_j\|k_j\|^2<\infty$ and $g\in D(M_r)$. Conversely, for $g\in D(M_r)$, reality of $rx$ gives $\langle M_rf,g\rangle_2=\langle f,M_rg\rangle_2$ for every $f\in D(M_r)$, hence $M_r^*g=M_rg$. Thus $M_r$ is self-adjoint with the displayed domain. [F5, F8, given, algebra]

If $r=0$, finite Hermite sums are dense in $L^2$ by [F3], and the operator graph norm is just the $L^2$ norm. Hence the image of $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is graph dense in $D(M_r)$. Step 1.2 identifies the restriction with $\phi_0(e)$, and scaling gives the same for $h=re$.
